steps.title: Resisting blows
steps.text: Toughness is the resistance of a stone to blows: chips, cracks, breaks. It is the second form of durability. It has nothing to do with hardness: a very hard stone can break with a sharp knock.

steps.title: Cleavage
steps.text: In some crystals, the bonds between atoms are weaker in certain planes. A blow can then split the stone along a smooth plane: this is cleavage. Diamond, topaz, fluorite and kunzite have cleavage planes. The lapidary must take them into account, and these stones are not worn where they are exposed.

steps.title: Fracture
steps.text: When there is no plane of weakness, or away from it, the stone breaks irregularly: this is fracture. It is called conchoidal when it forms arcs, like the inside of a shell (quartz, glass, obsidian), or splintery when it is fibrous (jade). Fracture helps recognize a rough stone or a glass imitation.

steps.title: Tough stones
steps.text: Some stones take blows very well. Jade is the toughest gem: its tangled fibres press tightly against each other. This is why it has been carved for thousands of years. A tough stone can be worn every day, even on an exposed piece such as a bracelet or a ring.

steps.title: The toughness scale
steps.text: Toughness is ranked from poor to exceptional: nephrite jade is exceptional, jadeite and corundum very good, diamond and quartz good, emerald and topaz fair, opal, fluorite and kunzite poor. Inclusions and fractures reduce the toughness of a stone: a heavily included emerald is more fragile than its hardness suggests.

steps.title: To remember
steps.text:
• Toughness and hardness are two different things: diamond is the hardest, but not the toughest.
• Cleavage: a split along a smooth plane. Fracture: an irregular chip.
• For jewellery worn every day, you need good toughness as much as good hardness.
